items.title: I can define psychological development and identify its three domains
items.what: Psychological development refers to an individual's changes in functioning across multiple domains, specifically emotional, cognitive, and social growth, and it continues throughout the entire lifespan.
items.why: Knowing the three domains allows students to categorise developmental changes correctly and avoid confusing, for example, cognitive development with social development.
items.example: A child learning to recognise when a friend is upset (emotional development), learning to add numbers (cognitive development), and learning to take turns in a game (social development) are three distinct but interconnected processes.

subtopic.name: Psychological Development Across the Lifespan
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces psychological development as a lifelong process encompassing emotional, cognitive, and social domains. It outlines the broad developmental periods from infancy through late adulthood and establishes that development follows a general trajectory that varies between individuals.
subtopic.why: Understanding that psychological development is continuous and lifelong helps students avoid the misconception that development ends in childhood or adolescence. It also provides the foundation for evaluating theories and evidence about how people change over time.

items.title: I can identify the seven developmental periods across the lifespan and their approximate age ranges
items.what: Developmental periods are broad age-based categories used to describe typical patterns of psychological change: infancy (0-12 months), toddlerhood (1-3 years), childhood (3-12 years), adolescence (12-19 years), young adulthood (19-35 years), middle adulthood (35-65 years), and late adulthood (65+ years).
items.why: These periods give a shared framework for discussing development, while the use of broad ranges rather than specific ages acknowledges that individuals develop at different rates.
items.example: A 14-year-old navigating questions about identity and peer relationships is in adolescence, whereas a 50-year-old reflecting on whether their career has been meaningful is in middle adulthood.

subtopic.why: Understanding that psychological development is continuous and lifelong helps students avoid the misconception that development ends in childhood or adolescence. It also provides the foundation for evaluating theories and evidence about how people change over time.

items.title: I can explain why developmental periods are given as broad ranges rather than specific ages
items.what: The timeline of psychological development varies between individuals, meaning no single age precisely marks when a developmental change occurs. Theories use ranges to capture the general population trend rather than predict exact outcomes.
items.why: Recognising individual variation prevents students from applying developmental frameworks too rigidly, and it is directly relevant to evaluating the limitations of theories like Piaget's.
items.example: Two children in the same Year 3 classroom (both aged 7-8) may differ in whether they have developed conservation, the understanding that a rolled-out ball of clay contains the same amount as a compact ball.

items.title: I can explain how the three domains of psychological development interact with one another
items.what: Emotional, cognitive, and social development do not occur in isolation; progress in one domain can support or depend on progress in another, making development a symbiotic process.
items.why: Understanding the interconnected nature of development helps explain why disruption in one area, such as poor emotional regulation, can affect outcomes in other areas, such as social relationships.
items.example: A child who develops empathy (emotional development) is better equipped to resolve conflict with peers (social development), which in turn may create opportunities for complex collaborative problem-solving (cognitive development).

items.title: I can define hereditary factors and environmental factors and give an example of each
items.what: Hereditary factors are genetically passed from biological parents to offspring and influence development from conception. Environmental factors arise from an individual's physical and social surroundings, including education, culture, peer groups, and early childhood experiences.
items.why: Being able to distinguish between these two types of factors is necessary for analysing case studies and applying the nature-nurture framework to real scenarios.
items.example: A child inheriting a genetic predisposition for depression is a hereditary factor; the child growing up in a household where a parent is frequently absent is an environmental factor.

subtopic.name: Nature versus Nurture
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the historical debate over whether hereditary factors (nature) or environmental factors (nurture) are the primary driver of psychological development. It concludes with the contemporary understanding that the two interact continuously and are rarely separable.
subtopic.why: The nature-nurture debate is foundational to all of psychology. Understanding that development results from the interaction of both factors, rather than one alone, allows students to critically evaluate claims about why people turn out the way they do.

items.title: I can describe the nature school of thought and its key claim about development
items.what: The nature school of thought holds that development is primarily determined by genetic composition and is largely predestined at birth, meaning traits such as intelligence and personality are inherited regardless of environmental experience.
items.why: Understanding this historical position allows students to identify its strengths, such as the observable heritability of physical traits, and its limitations, such as its inability to explain why identical twins can differ.
items.example: John Locke's 'tabula rasa' is the opposing view; a nature theorist would instead argue that a child born to two mathematically gifted parents is likely to show mathematical aptitude because of inherited traits, not teaching.

subtopic.why: The nature-nurture debate is foundational to all of psychology. Understanding that development results from the interaction of both factors, rather than one alone, allows students to critically evaluate claims about why people turn out the way they do.

items.title: I can describe the nurture school of thought and explain the concept of tabula rasa
items.what: The nurture school of thought holds that humans are born as a blank slate (tabula rasa) and are shaped entirely by their experiences, environment, and social surroundings. John Watson's behaviourism is a key example of this view.
items.why: Understanding the nurture position helps students recognise the significant role of environment and experience in shaping development, particularly through education, parenting, and socioeconomic status.
items.example: A child raised in a bilingual household who becomes fluent in two languages demonstrates the nurture position: the language environment, not genetic predisposition, produced that outcome.

subtopic.why: The nature-nurture debate is foundational to all of psychology. Understanding that development results from the interaction of both factors, rather than one alone, allows students to critically evaluate claims about why people turn out the way they do.

items.title: I can explain genetic predisposition and what it does and does not guarantee
items.what: Genetic predisposition is the increased likelihood of developing certain traits or conditions if certain environmental conditions are met. It raises the probability of an outcome but does not guarantee it.
items.why: Genetic predisposition is a nuanced concept that sits between pure nature and pure nurture; understanding it prevents students from overstating genetic determinism.
items.example: A person whose parent has clinical depression has a higher probability of developing depression than the general population, but may never develop it if their environment does not provide the triggering conditions.

subtopic.why: The nature-nurture debate is foundational to all of psychology. Understanding that development results from the interaction of both factors, rather than one alone, allows students to critically evaluate claims about why people turn out the way they do.

items.title: I can explain the contemporary understanding that nature and nurture interact to influence development
items.what: Contemporary psychology holds that hereditary and environmental factors are roughly equivalent in influence and operate in a continual, reciprocal relationship rather than independently. Genes can shape how individuals respond to environments, and environments can determine whether genetic predispositions are expressed.
items.why: This interactionist position is the current scientific consensus and is essential for answering exam questions that involve applying nature and nurture to case studies.
items.example: A child born with a warm, sociable temperament (hereditary) may be drawn to more social environments, which in turn further develops their social and emotional skills, demonstrating the reciprocal loop between nature and nurture.

items.title: I can define the biopsychosocial model and identify who developed it
items.what: The biopsychosocial model, developed by George Engel in 1977, is a holistic, interdisciplinary framework for understanding the human experience in terms of the interaction of biological, psychological, and social factors.
items.why: Knowing the origin and purpose of the model helps students understand why it was developed as an alternative to purely medical or biological approaches to health and development.
items.example: Engel argued that treating a patient with anxiety only with medication ignores the psychological coping strategies and social support networks that also determine whether the person recovers.

subtopic.name: The Biopsychosocial Model
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers George Engel's biopsychosocial model as a holistic, interdisciplinary framework that considers biological, psychological, and social factors as interacting influences on both mental wellbeing and psychological development.
subtopic.why: The biopsychosocial model provides a practical and comprehensive tool for analysing why individuals differ in their mental health and developmental outcomes, moving beyond single-cause explanations toward an understanding of cumulative, interacting factors.

items.title: I can define and give examples of biological, psychological, and social factors
items.what: Biological factors are internal genetic or physiological influences such as hormones, sleep, nutrition, and genetic predispositions. Psychological factors are internal mental processes including thoughts, beliefs, emotions, and coping skills. Social factors are external influences from relationships, community, culture, socioeconomic status, and family environment.
items.why: Correctly classifying factors into the three categories is a core skill required for case study analysis and short-answer questions throughout VCE Psychology.
items.example: In the case of Sam (15 years old), his family history of depression is a biological factor, his rumination about his ex-girlfriend is a psychological factor, and the breakup itself is a social factor.

subtopic.name: The Biopsychosocial Model
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers George Engel's biopsychosocial model as a holistic, interdisciplinary framework that considers biological, psychological, and social factors as interacting influences on both mental wellbeing and psychological development.
subtopic.why: The biopsychosocial model provides a practical and comprehensive tool for analysing why individuals differ in their mental health and developmental outcomes, moving beyond single-cause explanations toward an understanding of cumulative, interacting factors.

items.title: I can explain how the three biopsychosocial factors interact to influence mental wellbeing
items.what: Mental wellbeing is determined by the combined and interacting influence of biological, psychological, and social factors. No single factor alone is sufficient to cause high or low wellbeing, and disruption in one area affects the others.
items.why: Understanding the interactive nature of the model prevents students from attributing poor mental health to a single cause and supports the logic behind multi-pronged treatment approaches.
items.example: A person with a genetic predisposition to anxiety (biological) who also holds negative beliefs about their own competence (psychological) and has limited social support (social) is at significantly greater risk of poor mental wellbeing than someone with only one of these factors present.

subtopic.name: The Biopsychosocial Model
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers George Engel's biopsychosocial model as a holistic, interdisciplinary framework that considers biological, psychological, and social factors as interacting influences on both mental wellbeing and psychological development.
subtopic.why: The biopsychosocial model provides a practical and comprehensive tool for analysing why individuals differ in their mental health and developmental outcomes, moving beyond single-cause explanations toward an understanding of cumulative, interacting factors.

items.title: I can explain why a strictly biological approach to improving mental wellbeing is often insufficient
items.what: Because mental wellbeing is shaped by all three biopsychosocial factors, addressing only the biological dimension, such as prescribing medication, typically leaves psychological and social contributors unaddressed and is therefore unlikely to produce sustained improvement.
items.why: This point is a common exam application requiring students to evaluate treatment approaches and justify why holistic interventions are more appropriate.
items.example: A teenager prescribed antidepressants who continues to experience bullying at school (social) and uses avoidance as a coping strategy (psychological) is unlikely to achieve lasting improvement from medication alone.

subtopic.name: The Biopsychosocial Model
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers George Engel's biopsychosocial model as a holistic, interdisciplinary framework that considers biological, psychological, and social factors as interacting influences on both mental wellbeing and psychological development.
subtopic.why: The biopsychosocial model provides a practical and comprehensive tool for analysing why individuals differ in their mental health and developmental outcomes, moving beyond single-cause explanations toward an understanding of cumulative, interacting factors.

items.title: I can apply the biopsychosocial model to explain developmental outcomes
items.what: The biopsychosocial model can be applied to psychological development by identifying how biological, psychological, and social influences from infancy onward accumulate and interact to produce developmental outcomes across the lifespan.
items.why: Applying the model to development rather than just mental wellbeing demonstrates its interdisciplinary nature and is directly assessed in multi-mark questions.
items.example: An infant who is neglected (social) may experience disrupted brain development (biological) and develop low self-esteem (psychological), which then contributes to social isolation and difficulties finding employment in adulthood, illustrating a cascade of interacting biopsychosocial outcomes.

subtopic.why: The biopsychosocial model provides a practical and comprehensive tool for analysing why individuals differ in their mental health and developmental outcomes, moving beyond single-cause explanations toward an understanding of cumulative, interacting factors.

items.title: I can explain why one negative biopsychosocial influence alone is not sufficient to cause maladaptive development
items.what: Developmental outcomes are determined by the sum and interaction of all biopsychosocial influences encountered across the lifespan. A single negative factor can be buffered by positive influences in other domains, and a single positive factor cannot guarantee optimal development on its own.
items.why: This principle is frequently tested in exam scenarios where students must explain why a character who faces adversity in one area can still function well in others.
items.example: Adrian is a 30-year-old who struggles socially but performs well professionally. His positive biological health and psychological sense of job competence buffer the negative impact of his limited social development.

items.title: I can define emotional development and explain the role of theory of mind
items.what: Emotional development is the continuous, lifelong development of skills that allow individuals to control, express, and recognise emotions appropriately. Theory of mind is the ability to attribute and understand mental states, beliefs, and emotions in oneself and others, and it develops progressively from early childhood.
items.why: Theory of mind underpins empathy and emotional intelligence, making it a key concept for explaining how emotional competence develops over time.
items.example: A 4-year-old who cries when a friend takes their toy, but cannot understand why the friend wanted it, has not yet fully developed theory of mind. A 10-year-old who understands the friend may have taken it by accident has progressed further in theory of mind.

subtopic.name: Emotional and Social Development
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the theories used to explain emotional and social development across the lifespan, including attachment theory (Bowlby), theory of mind, emotional intelligence, and Erikson's psychosocial theory of development. It also addresses limitations of each theory.
subtopic.why: Emotional and social development are deeply interconnected and shape how individuals form relationships, manage emotions, and function within society throughout their lives. These theories are directly assessed in VCE Psychology and applied to case study analysis.

items.title: I can define emotional intelligence and explain how it relates to theory of mind
items.what: Emotional intelligence is the ability to monitor one's own and others' emotions and use that information to guide thoughts and behaviours. It is the outcome of a fully developed theory of mind and represents the mature endpoint of emotional development.
items.why: Emotional intelligence is the applied, adult-level expression of the emotional skills built progressively through theory of mind, making it useful for explaining differences between child and adult emotional responses.
items.example: Ruby, as an adult, no longer throws a tantrum when friends do not share. Instead she recognises a logical reason for their choice. This reflects emotional intelligence: she monitors the situation and regulates her response accordingly.

subtopic.name: Emotional and Social Development
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the theories used to explain emotional and social development across the lifespan, including attachment theory (Bowlby), theory of mind, emotional intelligence, and Erikson's psychosocial theory of development. It also addresses limitations of each theory.
subtopic.why: Emotional and social development are deeply interconnected and shape how individuals form relationships, manage emotions, and function within society throughout their lives. These theories are directly assessed in VCE Psychology and applied to case study analysis.

items.title: I can describe Bowlby's two categories of attachment style and their likely developmental outcomes
items.what: Bowlby proposed that attachment falls into two broad categories: secure attachment, where caregiver needs are consistently met, leading to trust and healthy emotional expression; and insecure attachment, where needs are inconsistently or rarely met, often leading to anxiety, inappropriate emotional expression, or difficulty forming relationships.
items.why: Attachment style in infancy is proposed to be a predictor of emotional outcomes across the lifespan, making it essential for explaining adult relationship difficulties in case study scenarios.
items.example: Marriane, who grew up with loving but busy parents and now struggles to voice her needs in relationships, may have experienced a form of insecure attachment where her emotional needs were not consistently addressed, leading to difficulty advocating for herself as an adult.

items.title: I can identify at least two limitations of attachment theory
items.what: Attachment theory has been criticised for failing to account for cross-cultural differences in caregiving practices and for providing insufficient explanation of what occurs between infancy and adulthood to produce the observed outcomes.
items.why: Evaluating theories is an explicit VCE skill. Knowing the limitations of attachment theory allows students to produce balanced evaluation responses rather than treating the theory as definitive.
items.example: In some cultures, infants are raised by extended family networks rather than a single primary caregiver, which challenges Bowlby's focus on the dyadic infant-caregiver bond as the primary driver of emotional development.

items.title: I can define social development and describe how it is influenced by parents and school
items.what: Social development is the continuous, lifelong development of skills, attitudes, relationships, and behaviours that enable individuals to interact with others and function as members of society. Parents and school both play significant roles: parents shape social development implicitly through mediating peer interactions and explicitly through teaching social rules, while school provides a structured environment for learning conflict management, turn-taking, and teamwork.
items.why: Social development is heavily shaped by external factors, making it a key example of nurture in action and a domain where intervention can meaningfully change developmental trajectories.
items.example: A child whose parents enrol them in team sports learns turn-taking, managing disappointment, and cooperation. A child not exposed to such environments may develop these skills later and through a less structured path.

items.title: I can describe Erikson's psychosocial theory, including the concept of a psychosocial crisis and at least four of the eight stages
items.what: Erikson proposed eight stages of psychosocial development spanning the entire lifespan. At each stage, an individual faces a psychosocial crisis, a tension between personal capabilities and societal expectations. Resolving the crisis leads to positive social development; failing to resolve it leads to negative outcomes that carry forward.
items.why: Erikson's theory is the primary framework for explaining social development across the lifespan in this unit and is applied directly in multi-mark exam questions.
items.example: An adolescent (12-19 years) who explores different identities and arrives at a clear sense of self resolves the Identity vs. Role Confusion crisis. One who never resolves it may remain uncertain about their values and identity into adulthood.

items.title: I can identify at least two limitations of Erikson's psychosocial theory
items.what: Erikson's theory is limited by its reliance on case studies and biographical data from Western populations, making it culturally biased. It has also not been updated since 1950 and does not account for major societal changes such as the influence of technology on identity formation.
items.why: As with attachment theory, evaluating Erikson's model is directly assessed and requires students to demonstrate both knowledge and critical thinking.
items.example: Social media has created new identity challenges for adolescents that did not exist in 1950. Erikson's model offers no framework for understanding how online identity expression relates to the Identity vs. Role Confusion crisis.

items.title: I can define cognitive development and explain why it is reliant on biological maturation
items.what: Cognitive development is the continuous, lifelong development of the ability to think, comprehend, and organise information from the internal and external environment. It depends partly on the maturation of neural networks, including the frontal lobe, which is responsible for planning, decision-making, working memory, and impulse control.
items.why: Linking cognitive development to brain maturation connects this subtopic to the broader unit theme of nature-nurture interaction and explains why certain cognitive abilities cannot simply be taught before the brain is ready.
items.example: The frontal lobe does not reach full maturity until approximately age 25, which is why adolescents show greater impulsivity and less effective long-term planning than adults, even when they understand the consequences of their actions intellectually.

subtopic.name: Cognitive Development and Piaget
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers cognitive development as a lifelong process underpinned by biological maturation of the brain, with particular focus on Piaget's four-stage theory of cognitive development, including the key achievements at each stage and the theory's limitations.
subtopic.why: Piaget's theory is one of the most influential and widely tested frameworks in developmental psychology. Understanding its stages, their defining cognitive milestones, and its limitations is directly assessed and provides a basis for evaluating experimental data about children's cognition.

items.title: I can describe the four stages of Piaget's theory of cognitive development, including their age ranges and key cognitive achievements
items.what: Piaget proposed four sequential stages: Sensorimotor (0-2 years), in which infants develop object permanence and goal-directed behaviour; Preoperational (2-7 years), in which children overcome egocentrism and centration and develop reversibility; Concrete Operational (7-12 years), in which children develop conservation, classification, and simple mental operations; and Formal Operational (12+ years), in which abstract thought, logic, and reasoning emerge.
items.why: The four stages and their defining cognitive milestones are core content for this topic and are assessed both as standalone knowledge and applied to experimental scenarios.
items.example: In a conservation task, a child in the Preoperational stage (e.g. age 5) will say a rolled-out piece of clay is larger than the original ball because it looks longer, whereas a child in the Concrete Operational stage (e.g. age 9) understands the amount remains the same regardless of shape.

subtopic.name: Cognitive Development and Piaget
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers cognitive development as a lifelong process underpinned by biological maturation of the brain, with particular focus on Piaget's four-stage theory of cognitive development, including the key achievements at each stage and the theory's limitations.
subtopic.why: Piaget's theory is one of the most influential and widely tested frameworks in developmental psychology. Understanding its stages, their defining cognitive milestones, and its limitations is directly assessed and provides a basis for evaluating experimental data about children's cognition.

items.title: I can explain what object permanence and conservation are and identify at which Piagetian stages they develop
items.what: Object permanence is the understanding that objects continue to exist even when out of sight, and it develops in the Sensorimotor stage. Conservation is the understanding that a property of an object, such as volume or mass, remains constant even when its appearance changes, and it develops in the Concrete Operational stage.
items.why: Object permanence and conservation are the two most frequently tested Piagetian concepts in VCE Psychology data analysis questions and case studies.
items.example: A 6-month-old infant cries when a toy is covered with a cloth because, lacking object permanence, they believe the toy no longer exists. A child in the Concrete Operational stage correctly identifies that pouring water from a tall thin glass into a short wide glass does not change the total volume.

Understanding its stages, their defining cognitive milestones, and its limitations is directly assessed and provides a basis for evaluating experimental data about children's cognition.

items.title: I can identify and apply the independent and dependent variables in a study testing Piaget's theory
items.what: In experiments testing Piaget's theory, the independent variable is typically the manipulation applied to the stimulus (such as the shape of clay), and the dependent variable is the children's perceptual response or judgment about the stimulus.
items.why: Identifying variables is a key science skill required across all VCE science subjects, and Piaget's conservation tasks provide a recurring context for this skill in Psychology.
items.example: In a study where 26 children are shown two equal balls of clay and one is then rolled out, the independent variable is the shape of the clay (changed by the researcher) and the dependent variable is the children's perception of whether the clay pieces are equal in size.

subtopic.why: Piaget's theory is one of the most influential and widely tested frameworks in developmental psychology. Understanding its stages, their defining cognitive milestones, and its limitations is directly assessed and provides a basis for evaluating experimental data about children's cognition.

items.title: I can evaluate Piaget's theory by identifying at least one strength and two limitations
items.what: A strength of Piaget's theory is that each stage can be tested through simple, observable tasks such as conservation experiments. Limitations include its failure to account for developmental diversity (that development is unique to each individual), its reliance on observational data from Piaget's own children, and its rigid assignment of ages to stages that does not accommodate individual variation.
items.why: Evaluation questions requiring students to assess the adequacy of Piaget's theory are a direct exam skill at both the apply-and-analyse and evaluate levels of the VCE Psychology study design.
items.example: If Piaget's theory were fully accurate, all 26 children in a classroom of the same age should answer a conservation task identically. The fact that answers vary across the class demonstrates the theory fails to account for individual differences in the rate of cognitive development.

Understanding its stages, their defining cognitive milestones, and its limitations is directly assessed and provides a basis for evaluating experimental data about children's cognition.

items.title: I can define maturation and explain how it determines the timing of development
items.what: Maturation is the biologically programmed process of growth that follows a fixed sequence and facilitates all aspects of development. Each individual has a unique developmental map determined at conception that sets out when specific developmental events will occur.
items.why: Maturation is the biological mechanism underlying both critical and sensitive periods, connecting this subtopic to the broader theme of nature and biological factors in development.
items.example: All children follow the same broad sequence of motor development, sitting before standing before walking, but the exact age at which each milestone occurs varies between individuals based on their unique maturation trajectory.

subtopic.name: Critical and Sensitive Periods
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the role of maturation and brain plasticity in determining windows of opportunity for skill acquisition. It distinguishes between critical periods, in which a skill must be acquired within a set window or may never develop, and sensitive periods, in which a skill is most efficiently acquired but can still develop later.
subtopic.why: Understanding critical and sensitive periods explains why early childhood experiences have such a profound and sometimes irreversible impact on development. This knowledge is also directly relevant to the case study of Genie, which provides evidence for and against the critical period hypothesis.

items.title: I can define brain plasticity and explain why it is higher during infancy and childhood
items.what: Brain plasticity is the brain's ability to physically change its structure in response to experience and learning. Plasticity is highest during infancy and early childhood because the brain is more malleable at this stage, allowing new pathways to form and strengthen more readily than in adulthood.
items.why: Plasticity is the neurological basis for why early experiences have such a strong influence on development and why critical and sensitive periods are concentrated in early life.
items.example: A child learning a second language at age 5 acquires it with native-like fluency because their brain readily forms the neural pathways required for the new language. An adult learning the same language must work against a less malleable brain, making the process slower and less complete.

subtopic.name: Critical and Sensitive Periods
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the role of maturation and brain plasticity in determining windows of opportunity for skill acquisition. It distinguishes between critical periods, in which a skill must be acquired within a set window or may never develop, and sensitive periods, in which a skill is most efficiently acquired but can still develop later.
subtopic.why: Understanding critical and sensitive periods explains why early childhood experiences have such a profound and sometimes irreversible impact on development. This knowledge is also directly relevant to the case study of Genie, which provides evidence for and against the critical period hypothesis.

items.title: I can define critical periods and explain what happens if the skill is not acquired within the window
items.what: A critical period is a narrow, rigid developmental window in which a specific function or skill must be acquired. If the skill is not acquired during this window, it may never fully develop or may remain severely impaired regardless of later exposure.
items.why: Critical periods represent some of the most significant and irreversible effects of the environment on development, making them important for understanding cases of extreme deprivation and the limits of later remediation.
items.example: First-language acquisition has a critical period roughly between birth and 5 years. Genie, who was isolated until age 13.5 and never spoken to, was later unable to fully develop grammar or verbal sentence production, suggesting these aspects of language had critical periods she had passed.

items.title: I can define sensitive periods and explain how they differ from critical periods
items.what: A sensitive period is the optimal developmental window for acquiring a skill in the fastest and most efficient way. Unlike critical periods, missing a sensitive period does not prevent the skill from developing; it simply means the process will be slower and more effortful, and the eventual level of mastery may be lower.
items.why: Distinguishing between critical and sensitive periods is a precise skill tested in both multiple-choice and short-answer questions, particularly around the use of words like 'must' versus 'optimally'.
items.example: Second-language acquisition has a sensitive period up to approximately age 12. A person who begins learning Italian at age 30 can still become proficient, but is unlikely to achieve native-speaker fluency in grammar and accent compared to someone who began as a child.

items.title: I can use the case study of Genie to evaluate the critical period hypothesis for language acquisition
items.what: The critical period hypothesis proposes that first-language acquisition must occur within a set developmental window or will not fully develop. Genie's case provides partial support: she could not develop grammar or produce verbal sentences after her critical period had passed, but she was able to learn individual words, suggesting some aspects of language have critical periods while others have sensitive periods.
items.why: Genie's case is the primary real-world evidence for discussing the critical period hypothesis in VCE Psychology and is commonly used in exam questions requiring students to both describe findings and evaluate a hypothesis.
items.example: Genie acquired a vocabulary of single words and two-word combinations after intervention, which suggests word learning does not have a strict critical period. However, her permanent inability to produce full sentences or understand intonation suggests these skills do have critical periods that had passed before she received language exposure.

items.title: I can compare critical and sensitive periods using a specific example of each
items.what: Critical periods are narrow, begin and end abruptly, and relate to skills that must be acquired within the window. Sensitive periods are broader, begin and end more gradually, and relate to skills that are simply easiest to acquire during the window but can still develop later.
items.why: Comparison questions requiring students to use both definitions alongside examples are a common exam format and require precise use of language, particularly 'must' for critical periods and 'optimal' for sensitive periods.
items.example: First-language grammar acquisition (critical period, roughly 0-5 years) must occur within the window or the skill may be permanently impaired, as seen in Genie. Second-language acquisition (sensitive period, roughly up to age 12) is most efficient in childhood, but Asanka, who began learning Spanish at 21, can still acquire it, just more slowly and with less likely fluency.
